# Hardness Amplification for Dynamic Binary Search Trees **Shunhua Jiang**
Columbia University, NY, USA **Victor Lecomte**
Stanford University, CA, USA **Omri Weinstein**
The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel **Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai**
The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel **Abstract** We prove direct-sum theorems for Wilber’s two lower bounds [Wilber, FOCS’86] on the cost of access sequences in the binary search tree (BST) model. These bounds are central to the question of dynamic optimality [Sleator and Tarjan, JACM’85]: the _Alternation_ bound is the only bound to have yielded online BST algorithms beating log_n_ competitive ratio, while the _Funnel_ bound has repeatedly been conjectured to exactly characterize the cost of executing an access sequence using the optimal tree [Wilber, FOCS’86, Kozma’16], and has been explicitly linked to splay trees [Levy and Tarjan, SODA’19]. Previously, the direct-sum theorem for the Alternation bound was known only when approximation was allowed [Chalermsook, Chuzhoy and Saranurak, APPROX’20, ToC’24]. We use these direct-sum theorems to amplify the sequences from [Lecomte and Weinstein, ESA’20] that separate between Wilber’s Alternation and Funnel bounds, increasing the Alternation and Funnel bounds while optimally maintaining the separation. As a corollary, we show that Tango trees [Demaine et al., FOCS’04] are optimal among any BST algorithms that charge their costs to the Alternation bound. This is true for _any_ value of the Alternation bound, even values for which Tango trees achieve a competitive ratio of _o_(loglog_n_) instead of the default _O_(loglog_n_). Previously, the optimality of Tango trees was shown only for a limited range of Alternation bound [Lecomte and Weinstein, ESA’20]. **2012 ACM Subject Classification** Theory of computation \(\rightarrow\) Data structures design and analysis; Theory of computation \(\rightarrow\) Online algorithms **Keywords and phrases** Data Structures, Amortized Analysis **Acknowledgements** This research was supported by the European Research Council (ERC) Starting grant CODY 101039914. This work was done in part while the authors (SJ, OW, SY) were visiting the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing, UC Berkeley. ### 1 Introduction Direct Sum theorems assert a lower bound on a certain complexity measure C of a _composed_1 problem \(f\circ g\) in terms of the individual complexities of _f_ and _g_, ideally of the form \(\mathcal{C}(f\circ g)\approx\mathcal{C}(f)+\mathcal{C}(g)\). Direct Sums have a long history in complexity theory, as they provide a _black-box_ technique for amplifying the hardness of computational problems \(\mathcal{C}(f^{\circ k})\unknown k\cdot\mathcal{C}(f)\), and are the most promising approach for proving several holy-grail lower bounds in complexity theory [23, 20, 35, 2, 24]. Moreover, a "tensorization" property of C under composition 1 Formally speaking, direct-sum problems pertain to the complexity of solving _k_ separate copies of a problem _f_, rather than computing a composed function of _k_ copies _g(f(x_1)_,...,f(xk_)), but it is common to refer to both variations of the _k_-fold problem as direct-sums [23].

## 2 Hardness Amplification for Dynamic Binary Search Trees

allows to "lift" the problem and leverage its asymptotic behavior (e.g., concentration), which is not present in the single-copy problem - this feature has been demonstrated and exploited in various models, including combinatorial Discrepancy [28, 38], Richness of data structure problems [33], decision trees [35] and rank [24] to mention a few. Despite their powerful implications, (strong) direct-sum scaling of composed problems are often simply false [34, 39, 37], and highly depend on the underlying computational model.

In this paper, we study direct sums in the _online BST model_, motivated by the _dynamic optimality_ conjecture of Sleator and Tarjan [40]. The dynamic optimality conjecture postulates the existence of an _instance optimal_ binary search tree algorithm (BST), namely, an online self- adjusting BST whose running time<sup>2</sup> matches the best possible running time _in hindsight_ for any sufficiently long sequence of queries. More formally, denoting by T(_X_) the operational time of a BST algorithm T on an access sequence \(X=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in[n]^m\) of keys to be searched, the conjecture says that there is an online BST T such that \(\forall X\), \(\mathcal{T}(X)\le O(\mathsf{OPT}(X))\), where \(\mathsf{OPT}(X):=min_{\mathcal{T}^\prime}\mathcal{T}'(X)\) denotes the optimal offline cost for _X_. In their seminal paper, Sleator and Tarjan [40] conjectured that _splay trees_ are _O_(1)-competitive; A more recent competitor, the _GreedyFuture_ algorithm [30, 15, 31], also forms a compelling candidate for constant-competitive dynamic optimality. However, the near-optimality of both Splay trees and GreedyFuture was proven only in special cases [41, 18, 32, 7, 8, 21, 10, 13], and they are not known to be _o_(log_n_)-competitive for general access sequences _X_ (note that every balanced BST is trivially _O_(log_n_)-competitive). After 35 years of active research, the best provable bound to date is an _O_(loglog_n_)-competitive BST, starting with _Tango trees_ [16], among other _O_(loglog_n_)-competitive BST algorithms [5, 42, 6]. Interestingly, this progress was made possible due the development of _lower bounds_ in the BST model, as we discuss next.

Indeed, a remarkable feature of the BST model--absent from general computational models (e.g., word-RAM)--is that it allows for nontrivial lower bounds on the search time of a _fixed_ query sequence _X_: In general models, lower bounds against a specific input _X_ do not make much sense as the best algorithm in hindsight can simply "store and read-off the answer" for _X_. Nevertheless, in the BST model, even an all-knowing binary search tree must pay the cost of traversing the root-to-leaf path to retrieve keys. For example, there are classical examples of deterministic access sequences (e.g., _bit-reversal_ sequence [43]) that require the worst case \(\Omega(mlogn)\) total search time. This feature is what makes instance-optimality in the BST model an intriguing possibility. Our work focuses on two classic lower bounds due to Wilber [43], the Alternation and Funnel bounds (a.k.a, Wilber’s first and second bounds), which are central to the aforementioned developments.

**The Alternation and Funnel Bounds.** Essentially all BST lower bounds are derived from a natural geometric interpretation of the access sequence _X_=(_X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>m</sub>_) as a point set on the plane, mapping the _i_th access _X<sub>i</sub>_ to point (_X<sub>i</sub>,i_) ([15, 22], see Figure 1). The earliest lower bounds on OPT(_X_) were proposed in an influential paper of Wilber [43]. The _alternation bound_ Alt<sub>T</sub>(_X_) counts the total number of left/right alternations obtained by searching the keys _X_=(_X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>m</sub>_) on a _fixed_ (static) binary search tree T , where alternations are summed up over all nodes \(v\in\mathcal{T}\) of the "reference tree" T (see Figure 3 and the formal definition in Section 2). Thus, the Alternation bound is actually a family of lower bounds, optimized by the choice of the reference tree T , and we henceforth define Alt(_X_):=max<sub>T</sub>Alt<sub>T</sub>(_X_). The Alternation bound plays a key role in the design and analysis of Tango trees and their variants [16, 42]. In fact, _all_ non-trivial _o_(log_n_)-competitive BST<tbc>

algorithms [16, 5, 42, 6, 11] rely on the Alternation bound.

In the same paper, Wilber proposed another lower bound--the _Funnel Bound_ Funnel(_X_)-- which is less intuitive and can be defined by the following process: Consider the geometric view \(\{(X_i,i)\}_{i\in[m]}\) of the simple "move-to-root" algorithm that simply rotates each searched key _X<sub>i</sub>_ to the root by a series of single rotations. Then Funnel(_X<sub>i</sub>,i_) is exactly the number of _turns_ on the path from the root to _X<sub>i</sub>_ right before it is accessed [1, 22]. The Funnel bound is then defined as \(\mathsf{Funnel}(X):=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathsf{Funnel}(X_i,i)\). This view emphasizes the _amortized_ nature of the Funnel bound: at any point, there could be linearly many keys in the tree that are only _one_ turn away from the root, so one can only hope to achieve this bound in some amortized fashion.

The Funnel bound has been repeatedly conjectured to tightly characterize the cost of an offline optimal algorithm [43, 25, 6, 27]. Recently, Lecomte and Weinstein [27] proved that the funnel bound is _rotation-invariant_, meaning that the bound is preserved when the geometric representation of the input sequence is rotated by 90 degrees. This property also holds for an optimal algorithm [15], giving another evidence that the Funnel bound might give a tight characterization of the cost of an offline optimal algorithm. While the Funnel bound does not have an algorithmic interpretation like Alt(_X_), Levy and Tarjan [29] recently observed interesting similarities between Splay trees and the Funnel bound. The core difficulty in converting Funnel(_X_) into a BST algorithm is its highly _amortized_ nature (also a feature of Splay trees), compared to the Alternation bound which gives a point-wise lower bound on the retrieval time of \(X_i\in X\). As such, understanding the mathematical properties of the Funnel bound is important in its own right.

**Access Sequence Composition and Known Direct-Sum Results.** Informally, Direct Sum theorems assert a lower bound on the complexity measure of solving _R_ copies of a problem in a given computational model, in terms of the cost of solving a single copy, ideally \(C(f^{\circ R})\unknown\Omega(R)\cdot C(f)\), where \(f^{\circ R}\) denotes certain _R_-copy _composed_ problem. Indeed, the precise notion of composition we use here (a-la [9]) is crucial, as direct-sum theorems are subtle and often turn out to be _false_ [34].

A natural definition of sequence-composition in the BST model was introduced by Chalermsook et al. [9]. Let \(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(\ell)}\) be a sequence of \(\ell\) access sequences where \(X^{(i)}\in[n_i]^{m_i}\). That is, each sequence _X_<sup>(_i_)</sup> has _n<sub>i</sub>_ keys and _m<sub>i</sub>_ accesses where \(m:=\sum_im_i,n:=\sum_in_i\). We view each sequence _X_<sup>(_i_)</sup> as the _i_th queue where we dequeue elements by the order of the sequence _X_<sup>(_i_)</sup> (i.e., in FIFO order). Let \(\widetilde{X}\in[\ell]^m\) be a sequence with keys in \([\ell]\) such that every \(j\in[\ell]\) appears exactly _m<sub>j</sub>_ times. We can view \(\widetilde{X}\) as a _template_ which defines the ordering of dequeue operations among the \(\ell\) queues. We define the _composed sequence_ \(X:=\widetilde{X}(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(\ell)})\in[n]^m\) as follows. For each _t_=1 to _m_, \(X_t:=q_t+\sum_{i<\widetilde{X}_t}n_i\) where _q<sub>t</sub>_ is the next element dequeued from \(X^{(\widetilde{X}_t)}\). We refer the reader to Section 2 for the precise definition.

The direct sum results for the optimal cost are well understood with applications to proving non-trivial bounds of binary search trees. In [9], they prove (approximate) _subadditivity_ of the optimal cost on composed sequences. That is,

The subadditivity of optimal cost finds application in proving the linear optimal bounds for "grid" sequences, and a strong separation in the hierarchy of _lazy finger bounds_ [9]. On the other hand, [6] recently proved _superadditivity_ of the optimal cost on composed sequences.

\(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\le 3\cdot\mathsf{OPT}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{OPT}\big(X^{(j)}\big).\)

That is, \(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge\mathsf{OPT}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{OPT}\big(X^{(j)}\big).\) (1) The superadditivity of optimal cost finds an application in designing a new _O_(loglog_n_)- competitive online BST algorithm based on purely geometric formulation [6]. However, the direct sum results for Wilber’s bounds are poorly understood despite their importance to the pursuit of dynamic optimality. The only published work that we are aware of is the approximate subadditivity of the Alternation bound [6]. That is, they proved that \(\mathsf{Alt}(X)\le 4\cdot\mathsf{Alt}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+8\cdot\sum_j\mathsf{Alt}\big(X^{(j)}\big)+O(|X|).\) (2) Their proof is quite involved, and it is based on geometric arguments and the probabilistic method. This finds applications in proving the separation between the Alternation and Funnel bounds. In [6], they used approximate subadditivity of the Alternation bound (Equation (2)) to prove a near-optimal separation between the Alternation and Funnel bounds. That is, they constructed a sequence _Y_ such that the gap between Alt(_Y_) and Funnel(_Y_) is as large as \(\Omega(\frac{loglogn}{logloglogn})\). This gap is nearly optimal because the upper bound of Tango tree [16] implies that the gap must be _O_(loglog_n_). This gap has been closed by an independent work by Lecomte and Weinstein [27], proving the optimal separation between the Alternation and Funnel bounds. That is, they constructed an instance _Y_ such that the gap between Alt(_Y_) and Funnel(_Y_) is as large as \(\Omega(loglogn)\). Furthermore, [6] also used the approximate subadditivity of the Alternation bound (Equation (2)) to prove the \(\Omega(\frac{loglogn}{logloglogn})\) gap between Alt(_Y_) and cGB(_Y_) where cGB(_Y_) denotes the _Consistent Guillotine Bound_ (cGB), a lower bound measure that is an extension of Alt(_Y_). ### 1.1 Our Results We prove that the Alternation bound is subadditive whereas the Funnel bound is superadditive for composed sequences. More precisely, we prove the following theorem. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 1** (Direct-Sum Theorem for Wilber’s Bounds)**.** _Let_ \(X:=\widetilde{X}(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(l)})\) _be a composed sequence. Then_ \(\mathsf{Alt}(X)\le\mathsf{Alt}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Alt}\big(X^{(j)}\big)+O(|X|)\)_, and_ \(\mathsf{Funnel}(X)\ge\mathsf{Funnel}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Funnel}\big(X^{(j)}\big)-O(|X|).\) Our proof of the subadditivity of the Alternation bound is simpler and yields stronger bounds than the proof in [6] (Theorem 3.6 in their arXiv version). Direct sum theorems are a natural black-box tool for hardness amplification, as they effectively reduce complex lower bounds to a simpler "one-dimensional" problem. Indeed, as a showcase application, we use the base-case separation proved in [27] along with Theorem 1 to amplify both Wilber’s bounds. Let Alt(_X_):=Alt(_X)/|X_|, and Funnel(_X_):=Funnel(_X)/|X_|. They proved that there is a sequence _Y_ such that \(\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(Y)\le O(1),\text{but}\)
\(\overline{\mathsf{Funnel}}(Y)\ge\Omega(loglogn).\)

Note that the sequence _Y_ is _easy_ w.r.t. the Alteration bound since \(\overline{\text{Alt}}(Y)\le O(1)\). We use the sequence _Y_ as a base-case and apply Theorem 1 to construct _hard_ sequence w.r.t. the funnel bound while maintaining the separation as in the following theorem <sup>3</sup>.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 2** (Hardness Amplification)**.** _There is a constant K\>_0 _such that for any n of the form_ 2<sup>2_r_</sup> _and any power-of-two_ \(R\le\frac{logn}{K}\) _, there is a sequence_ \(Y_n^{\circ R}\in[n]m^{\prime\prime}\) _with_ \(m'\le poly(n)\) _such that_

\(\overline{\text{Alt}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\le O(R)\overline{\text{Funnel}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\ge\Omega\big(Rlog\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big).\)

**Remark 1.** We emphasize that the approximate subadditivity of the Alteration bound (Equation (2)) is not sufficient for such hardness amplification. On the other hand, one could also use the superadditivity of the optimal cost (Equation (1)) instead of the Funnel bound to prove hardness amplification.

**Tightness of the Separation.** As a corollary of Theorem 2, we can derive the following trade-offs between the multiplicative and additive factors for the Alteration bound.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 3.** _Let_ \(\alpha,\beta:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\) _be any functions such that some BST algorithm achieves an amortized cost of_ \(\alpha(n)\overline{\text{Alt}}(X)+\beta(n)\) _for all access sequences X over n keys. Then_ \(\alpha(n)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\beta(n)}\big)\big)\).

As we discuss below, the trade-offs are tight with the matching upper bounds from Tango Trees (which can be derived directly from Tango trees). For convenience, we present self-contained BST algorithms with the matching upper bounds.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 4.** _There is a BST algorithm that takes an integer_ \(k\le logn\) _as a parameter and serve the sequence_ \(X=(X_1,\cdots,X_m)\) _with the total access time of_

\(O\big(\big(\text{Alt}(X)+m\cdot\frac{logn}{k}\big)\cdot(logk+1)\big).\)

We prove Lemma 4 in Appendix A.

In this algorithm, the additive cost is \(\Theta\big(\frac{lognlogk}{k}\big)\) and multiplicative cost \(\Theta(logk)\). By Theorem 3, if \(\beta(n)=\Theta\big(\frac{lognlogk}{k}\big)\), then we have

\(\alpha(n)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\beta(n)}\big)\big)=\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{k}{logk}\big)\big)=\Omega(logk),\)

so our trade-off is optimal for any sufficiently large \(k\le logn\).

**Optimality of Tango Trees.** As another corollary of Theorem 2, we prove the optimality of Tango Trees among any algorithm charging its cost to Wilber’s Alteration bound for all values of the <o>Alt</o>(_X_). Note that \(\overline{\text{Alt}}(X)\le O(logn)\). Previously, the optimality of Tango trees is known only when <o>Alt</o>(_X_)=_O_(1) [27].

The basic idea of Tango Trees is to "mimic" Wilber’s alternation bound via a BST, by dynamically maintaining a partition of the reference tree T into _disjoint paths_, formed by designating, for each node \(x\in\mathcal{T}\) , the unique "preferred" descendant in T (left or right) which

was _accessed most recently_. Since each "preferred path" has length \(|p|\le\mathrm{depth}(\mathcal{T})\le\mathrm{log}n\), every _path_ can itself be stored in a BST, so assuming these paths can be dynamically maintained (under split and joins), searching for the predecessor of a key _x<sub>i</sub> inside_ each path only takes _O_(loglog_n_) time, until the search "falls-off" the current preferred path and switches to a different one. The key observation is that this "switch" can be charged to Alt<sub>T</sub>(_X_), as it certifies a new alternation in Wilber’s lower bound, hence OPT must pay for this move as well. This elegant argument directly leads to the aforementioned \(O(\mathrm{loglog}n)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(X)\) search time.

The analysis of Tango trees relies on charging the algorithm’s cost to the Alternation bound. One may ask if the bound can be improved using a clever algorithm (not necessarily Tango trees) so that we can charge _o_(loglog_n_) factor to the Alternation bound. Unfortunately, the answer is no as there are known examples of access sequences \(\tilde{X}\) with \(\mathsf{Alt}(\tilde{X})=O(m)\) but \(\mathsf{OPT}(\tilde{X})=\Theta(m\mathrm{loglog}n)\) [27, 6]. In light of this, Tango trees are indeed off by a factor \(\Theta(\mathrm{loglog}n)\) from \(\mathsf{Alt}(\tilde{X})\). Interestingly, when \(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\unknown m\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{2^{o(\mathrm{loglog}n)}}\) , one can do somewhat better. Let <o>OPT</o>(_X_):=OPT(_X)/|X_|. The Tango tree, presented by [16] (see the discussion in their Section 1.5), has a competitive ratio of

\(O\big(1+\mathrm{log}\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{\mathsf{OPT}(X)}\big)=o(\mathrm{loglog}n).\) (3)

The condition that allows _o_(loglog_n_)-competitiveness is rather narrow: the amortized optimal cost <o>OPT</o>(_X_) must be very close to log_n_ to achieve _o_(loglog_n_)-competitiveness. Can we achieve _o_(loglog_n_)-competitiveness with a wider range of <o>OPT</o>(_X_) using Alt(_X_)?

Unfortunately, the answer is no. More generally, we prove a matching lower bound: the competitive ratio of any BST algorithm based on the Alternation bound must be at least \(\Omega(\mathrm{log}\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{\mathsf{OPT}(X)})\), matching to the upper bound of the Tango tree by Equation (3). More precisely, we prove the following theorem whose proof is a small modification of the proof in Theorem 3.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 5.** _Let_ \(\alpha:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\) _be any function such that some BST algorithm achieves an amortized cost of_ \(\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(X)\big)\cdot\big(\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(X)+1\big)\) _for all access sequences X over n keys. Then_ \(\alpha(n,s)\ge\Omega\big(\mathrm{log}\big(\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{s}\big)\big)\).

As a corollary of Theorem 5,<sup>4</sup> the lower bound of \(\Omega(\mathrm{log}\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{\mathsf{OPT}(X)})\) follows by setting _s_ to be within constant factor of <o>OPT</o>(_X_). This holds for every BST algorithm based on the Alternation bound. With the matching upper bound by Equation (3), Tango tree optimally utilizes the Alternation bound.

### 1.2 Further Related Work

Splay trees and GreedyFuture are prime candidates for the dynamic optimality conjecture since they both satisfy many important properties of dynamic trees including static optimality [40], working-set property [40, 19], dynamic finger property [14, 12], and more (see the surveys [22, 25] for an overview of the results in the field). Although they are not yet known

For example, both Splay trees and GreedyFuture are dynamically optimal for _sequential access_ sequences [18, 19]. For _deque sequences_, Splay trees are \(O(\alpha^*(n))\)-competitive [32] whereas GreedyFuture is \(O(\alpha(n))\)-competitive [10]. Here, \(\alpha(n)\) denotes the inverse Ackermann function and \(\alpha^*(n)\) is the iterated function of \(\alpha(n)\). The sequential and deque sequences are special cases of the _pattern-avoiding access_ sequences [8]. For any fixed-size pattern, GreedyFuture is \(O(2^{(1+o(1))\alpha(n)})\)-competitive for pattern-avoiding access sequences [13]. It was shown recently that an optimal BST algorithm takes _O(n_) total cost for any fixed pattern [3] and there is an optimal algorithm for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences [**?**]. The bounds for specific classes of patterns can be improved if preprocessing is allowed [8, 21] (i.e., the initial tree can be set before executing the online search sequences). Recently, a slight modification of GreedyFuture was shown to be \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-competitive [11]. An important application of GreedyFuture (or any competitive online BSTs) includes adaptive sorting using treesort [4, 13] and heapsort [26].

The lower bounds in the literature other than Wilber’s bounds include the _maximum independent rectangle_ and _SignedGreedy_ bounds [15], which subsume Wilber’s Alternation and Funnel bounds. A similar lower bound was presented by Derryberry et al. [17]. Recently, _Guillotine_ Bound [6] was introduced, which is a generalization of Wilber’s Alternation bound. Unfortunately, it is unclear how to design an algorithm that utilizes these bounds. Recently, Sadeh and Kaplan [36] proved that the competitive ratio of GreedyFuture cannot be less than 2 for the multiplicative factor, or _o(m_loglog_n_) for the additive factor.

## 1.3 Paper Organization

We first describe terminologies and notations in Section 2. We prove the direct-sum results for Wilber’s bounds (Theorem 1) in Section 3. In Section 4, we prove the hardness amplification of Wilber’s bounds while maintaining their separation (Theorem 2) and we also prove Theorem 3. We prove the superadditivity of the Funnel Bound in Section 5.

## 2 Preliminaries

We follow notations and terminologies from [27].

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 6** (access sequence)**.** _An access sequence is a finite sequence_ \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_m)\in S^m\) _of values from a finite set of keys_ \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}\)_. Usually, we let S_:=[_n]._

To make our definitions and proofs easier, we will work directly in the geometric representation of access sequences as (finite) sets of points in the plane R<sup>2</sup>.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 7** (geometric view)**.** _Any access sequence_ \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_m)\in S^m\) _can be represented as the set of points_ \(G_X:=\{(X_t,t)|t\in[m]\}\)_, where the x-axis represents the key and the y-axis represents time (see Figure 1)._

By construction, in _G<sub>X</sub>_, no two points share the same _y_-coordinate. We will say such a set has "distinct _y_-coordinates". In addition, we note that it is fine to restrict our attention to sequences _X_ without repeated values.<sup>5</sup> The geometric view _G<sub>X</sub>_ of such sequences also

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 8** (_x_- and _y_-coordinates)**.** _For a point_ \(p\in\mathbb{R}^2\)_, we will denote its x- and y- coordinates as p.x and p.y. Similarly, we define_ \(P.x:=\{p.x|p\in P\}\) _and_ \(P.y:=\{p.y|p\in P\}\).

We start by defining the _mixing value_ of two sets: a notion of how many two sets of numbers are interleaved. It will be useful in defining both the alternation bound and the funnel bound. We define it in a few steps.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 9** (mixing string)**.** _Given two disjoint finite sets of real numbers L,R, let_ mix(_L,R_) _be the string in_ {L,R}<sup>∗</sup> _that is obtained by taking the union_ \(L\cup R\) _in increasing order and replacing each element from L by_ L _and each element from R by_ R_. For example,_ mix({2,3,8},{1,5})=`RLLRL`.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 10** (number of switches)**.** _Given a string_ \(s\in\{\mathtt{L},\mathtt{R}\}^*\)_, we define_ #switches(_s_) _as the number of side switches in s. Formally,_

\(\#\text{switches}(s):=\#\{t|s_t\neq s_{t+1}\}.\)

_For example,_ #switches(`LLLRLL`)=2_. Note that if we insert characters into s,_ #switches(_s_) _can only increase._

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 11** (mixing value)**.** _Let_ mixValue(_L,R_):=#switches(mix(_L,R_)) _(see Figure 2)._

The mixing value has some convenient properties, which we will use later:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Fact 12** (properties of mixValue)**.** _Function_ mixValue(_L,R_) _is:_

**(a)** _symmetric:_ mixValue(_L,R_)=mixValue(_R,L_);

**(b)** _monotone: if_ \(L_1\subseteq L_2\) _and_ \(R_1\subseteq R_2\)_, then_ \(\text{mixValue}(L_1,R_1)\le\text{mixValue}(L_2,R_2)\);

**(c)** _superadditive under concatenation: if_ \(L_1,R_1\subseteq(-\infty,x]\) _and_ \(L_2,R_2\subseteq[x,+\infty)\)_, then_ \(\text{mixValue}(L_1\cup L_2,R_1\cup R_2)\ge\text{mixValue}(L_1,R_1)+\text{mixValue}(L_2,R_2)\).

_Finally,_ \(\text{mixValue}(L,R)\le 2\cdot\text{min}(|L|,|R|)+1\).

The definitions of Wilber’s Alternation and Funnel bounds (Alt(_X),_Funnel(_X_)) are standard in the literature.

We now give precise definitions of Wilber’s two bounds.<sup>6</sup>

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 13** (alternation bound)**.** _Let P be a point set with distinct y-coordinates, and let_ T _be a binary search tree over the values P.x. We define_ Alt<sub>T</sub>(_P_) _using the recursive structure of_ T_. If_ T _is a single node, let_ Alt<sub>T</sub>(_P_):=0_. Otherwise, let_ T<sub>L</sub> _and_ T<sub>R</sub> _be the left and right subtrees at the root. Partition P into two sets_ \(P_\mathrm{L}:=\{p\in P|p.x\in\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{L}\}\) _and_ \(P_\mathrm{R}:=\{p\in P|p.x\in\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{R}\}\) _and consider the quantity_ mixValue(_P_<sub>L</sub>_.y,P_<sub>R</sub>_.y), which describes how much P_<sub>L</sub> _and P_<sub>R</sub> _are interleaved with time (we call each switch between P_<sub>L</sub> _and P_<sub>R</sub> _a “preferred child alternation”). Then_

\(\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(P):=\mathrm{mixValue}(P_\mathrm{L}.y,P_\mathrm{R}.y)+\mathsf{Alt}_{\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{L}}(P_\mathrm{L})+\mathsf{Alt}_{\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{R}}(P_\mathrm{R}).\) (4)

_The alternation bound is then defined as the maximum over all trees:_

\(\mathsf{Alt}(P):=\mathrm{max}_\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(P).\)

_In addition, for an access sequence X, let_ Alt<sub>T</sub>(_X_):=Alt<sub>T</sub>(_G<sub>X</sub>_) _and_ Alt(_X_):=Alt(_G<sub>X</sub>)._

For the next few definitions, it is helpful to refer back to Figure 4. In particular, _F_<sub>L</sub>(_P,p_) and _F_<sub>R</sub>(_P,p_) (the left and right funnel) correspond to the points marked with L and R.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 14** (left and right funnel)**.** _Let P be a point set. For each_ \(p\in P\)_, we say that access_ \(q\in P\) _is in the left (resp. right) funnel of p within P if q is to the lower left (resp. lower right) of p and_ \(\square pq\) _is empty. Formally, let_

\(F_\mathrm{L}(P,p):=\{q\in P|q.y<p.y\wedge q.x<p.x\wedge P\cap\square pq=\{p,q\}\}\)

_and_

\(F_\mathrm{R}(P,p):=\{q\in P|q.y<p.y\wedge q.x>p.x\wedge P\cap\square pq=\{p,q\}\}.\)

_We will collectively call_ \(F_\mathrm{L}(P,p)\cup F_\mathrm{R}(P,p)\) _the funnel of p within P._

## 3 Effect of Composition on Wilber’s bounds

We prove Theorem 1 in this section. Namely, we show that Wilber’s bounds act nicely under composition, allowing us to boost the separation between them in Section 4. We divide the proofs into the following two theorems.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 19 (subadditivity of Alt).** _Let_ \(X:=\widetilde{X}(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(l)})\) _be a composed sequence with_ \(|X^{(1)}|=\cdots=|X^{(l)}|\).<sup>7</sup> _Then_

\(\mathsf{Alt}(X)\le\mathsf{Alt}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Alt}\big(X^{(j)}\big)+O(m).\)

We prove Theorem 19 in Section 3.1.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 20 (superadditivity of Funnel).** _Let_ \(X:=\widetilde{X}(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(l)})\) _be a composed sequence. Then_

\(\mathsf{Funnel}(X)\ge\mathsf{Funnel}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Funnel}\big(X^{(j)}\big)-O(m).\)

We prove Theorem 20 in Section 5.

### 3.1 Subadditivity of the alternation bound

We prove Theorem 19 in this section.

### Proof plan

We will show that for any binary search tree T over \(S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_l\),

\(\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(X)\le\mathsf{Alt}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Alt}\big(X^{(j)}\big)+O(m).\)

We will do this by

decomposing T into the corresponding binary trees \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) over [_l_] and T_<sub>j</sub>_ over _S<sub>j</sub>_ for all _j_; \(\blacksquare\) classifying preferred child alternations in T into 4 types, which correspond to either \(\blacksquare\) alternations in \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\), \(\blacksquare\) alternations in T_<sub>j</sub>_ for some _j_, \(\blacksquare\) or to some other events that happen at most _O(m_) times in aggregate. That is, we will show that

\(\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(X)\le\mathsf{Alt}_\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\big(\widetilde{X}\big)+\sum_j\mathsf{Alt}_{\mathcal{T}_j}\big(X^{(j)}\big)+O(m).\)

#### 3.1.1 Decomposing the tree

For a tree T , we write \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) if _x_ is a descendent of _b_ in T , and we write \(S\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) if \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) for all \(x\in S\).

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 21.** _Let_ T_<sub>j</sub> be the unique binary search tree over S<sub>j</sub> such that if_ \(b,x\in S_j\) _and_ \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) _then_ \(x\prec_{\mathcal{T}_j}b\).

<sup>7</sup> We make this assumption so that the proof is simpler.

T_<sub>j</sub>_ is constructed by running the following recursive algorithm, which builds a tree T<sub>out</sub>:

Start at the root of T , and let _x_ be the current node.

If \(x\in S_j\), then

make _x_ the root of T<sub>out</sub>;

form _x_’s left subtree in T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on _x_’s left subtree in T ;

form _x_’s right subtree in T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on _x_’s right subtree in T .

If \(x\unknown\in S_j\) then since _S<sub>j</sub>_ is contiguous, at most one of _x_’s left and right subtrees in T can contain elements from _S<sub>j</sub>_.

If there is one such subtree, form T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on it.

Otherwise let T<sub>out</sub> be the empty tree.

This algorithm clearly has the desired properties:

Clearly, by construction, T_<sub>j</sub>_ is a binary search tree and its set of keys is _S<sub>j</sub>_.

If \(b,x\in S_j\) and \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\), then \(x\prec_{\mathcal{T}_j}b\), because the only way to get to _x_ is to first pass through _b_, add it as a root of the current subtree, then recurse on _b_’s subtree that contains _x_, which eventually adds _x_ to T_<sub>j</sub>_ as a descendent of _b_.

T_<sub>j</sub>_ is unique since the only nontrivial choice the algorithm makes is to add _x_ as a root, but this is necessary since it must be an ancestor of all of the keys that later get added to this part of T_<sub>j</sub>_.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 22.** _Let_ \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) _be the unique binary search tree over_ [_l_] _such that if_ \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) and \(S_{jb},S_{jx}\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) _then_ \(j_x\prec_\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}j_b\).

\(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) is constructed by running the following recursive algorithm, which builds a tree T<sub>out</sub>:

Start at the root of T , and let _x_ be the current node.

If _j<sub>x</sub>_ hasn’t already been seen earlier in the algorithm (which happens iff _x_ is the lowest common ancestor of all of _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_ in T ), then

make _j<sub>x</sub>_ the root of T<sub>out</sub>;

form _j<sub>x</sub>_’s left subtree in T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on _x_’s left subtree in T ;

form _j<sub>x</sub>_’s right subtree in T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on _x_’s right subtree in T .

If _j<sub>x</sub>_ has already been seen earlier in the algorithm, then some ancestor of _x_ was also in _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_, and _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_ is contiguous, so _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_ must contain either _x_’s entire left subtree, or _x_’s entire right subtree. That means that at most one of _x_’s subtrees can contain elements \*not\* in _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_.

If there is one such subtree, form T<sub>out</sub> by recursing on it.

Otherwise, let T<sub>out</sub> be the empty tree.

This algorithm clearly has the desired properties:

Clearly, by construction, \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) is a binary search tree and its set of keys is [_l_].

If \(x\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) and \(S_{jb},S_{jx}\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) then:

We can assume \(j_x\neq j_b\) and thus \(x\neq b\), otherwise the claim is trivially true.

Since \(S_{jb}\prec_\mathcal{T}b\), _b_ must be the lowest common ancestor of all of _S<sub>jb</sub>_ in T , so _j<sub>b</sub>_ gets added to \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) when the algorithm is looking at node _b_.

Also, since \(S_{j_x}\prec_\mathcal{T}b\) and \(j_x\neq j_b\), that means that all the elements from _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_ are descendents of _b_, so _j<sub>x</sub>_ will be added to \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) in one of the recursive branches launched when looking at _b_.

Therefore _j<sub>x</sub>_ will be a descendent of _j<sub>b</sub>_ in \(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\).

\(\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\) is unique since the only nontrivial choice the algorithm makes is to add _j<sub>x</sub>_ as root when it first sees an element from _S<sub>j<sub>x</sub></sub>_, but this is necessary since for any _j_ which will eventually be added to this part of the tree, _S<sub>j</sub>_ must have been completely contained in _x_’s subtree, and therefore _j<sub>x</sub>_ must be an ancestor of _j_.

## 4.2 Optimality of Tango Trees

We are ready to prove Theorem 3. \(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 26** (Restatement of Theorem 3)**.** _Let_ \(\alpha,\beta:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\) _be any functions and let A be some BST algorithm. Denote the amortized cost of A on an access sequence X as <o>A</o>(X). Suppose that for all access sequences X over n keys, we have_

\(\overline{A}(X)\le\alpha(n)\overline{\text{Alt}}(X)+\beta(n).\)

_Then_ \(\alpha(n)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\beta(n)}\big)\big)\) _for infinitely many values of n._ **Proof.** In fact we will show that the result holds under the weaker assumption that the theorem holds for the _optimal_ amortized cost: \(\overline{\text{OPT}}(X)\le\alpha(n)\overline{\text{Alt}}(X)+\beta(n).\) The above inequality must in particular hold for the access sequence \(Y_n^{\circ R}\) from Theorem 2, where we let _R_ be the largest power of two such that \(R\le\beta(n)\). This gives us

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \overline{\text{OPT}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\le\alpha(n)\overline{\text{Alt}}(X)+\beta(n)\le O(R(\alpha(n)+1)) \\ \overline{\text{OPT}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\ge\Omega\big(\overline{\text{Funnel}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\big)\ge\Omega\big(Rlog\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big). \end{array}\right.\)

Combining these inequalities, we obtain

\(R(\alpha(n)+1)\ge\Omega\big(Rlog\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big)\Longrightarrow\alpha(n)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\beta(n)}\big)\big)\) (where the implication uses the fact that \(\alpha(n)\ge 1\)). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

### Optimal Trade-off

The matching trade-offs for \(\alpha(n)\) and \(\beta(n)\) follows from Tango trees [16] as discussed in the introduction. We provide an alternate proof by designing an algorithm parameterized by _k_ in

Lemma 4 for completeness. That is, we describe a family of simple algorithms parameterized by \(k\le logn\) that gives a matching upper bound of

\(O\big(\big(\mathsf{Alt}(X)+m\cdot\frac{logn}{k}\big)\cdot(logk+1)\big).\)

In this algorithm, the fixed cost is \(\beta(n)=\Theta\big(\frac{lognlogk}{k}\big)\) and multiplicative factor \(\alpha(n)=\Theta(logk)\). We just proved that any algorithm with fixed cost \(\beta(n)\) must have

\(\alpha(n)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\beta(n)}\big)\big)=\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{k}{logk}\big)\big)=\Omega(logk),\)

so our trade-off is optimal for any sufficiently large \(k\le logn\).

_Note:_ The trade-off above suggests that there is some leeway in the other direction, i.e. we could have an algorithm with the same multiplicative factor of _O_(log_k_) but a reduced fixed cost of \(\frac{logn}{(logk)^C}\) for any _C\>_1 we choose. And this is indeed the case: we simply need to change variables

\(k':=k^{1/C}\Longrightarrow O\big((logk)\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(X)+\frac{lognlogk}{k}\big)\le O\big((logk')\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(X)+\frac{logn}{(k')^{C-o(1)}}\big).\)

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Theorem 27** (Restatement and full version of Theorem 5)**.** _Let_ \(\alpha:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 1}\) _be any function and let A be some BST algorithm. Denote the amortized cost of A on an access sequence X as <o>A</o>(X). Suppose that for all access sequences X over n keys, we have_

\(\overline{A}(X)\le\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(X)\big)\cdot\big(\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(X)+1\big).\)

_Then_ \(\alpha(n,s)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{s}\big)\big)\) _for infinitely many values of n, and (for each such n) for a set of values for s that ranges from O_(1) _to_ \(\Omega(logn)\) _and are spaced by at most a constant factor._

**Proof.** Again, we will show that the result holds under the weaker assumption that the theorem holds for the _optimal_ amortized cost:

\(\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(X)\le\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(X)\big)\cdot\big(\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(X)+1\big).\)

The above inequality must in particular hold for the access sequence \(Y_n^{\circ R}\) from Theorem 2, for any power-of-two _R_. This gives us

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \overline{\mathsf{OPT}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\le\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(Y_n^{\circ R})\big)\cdot\big(\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(Y_n^{\circ R})+1\big)\le O\big(R\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(Y_n^{\circ R})\big)\big) \\ \overline{\mathsf{OPT}}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\ge\Omega\big(\mathsf{Funnel}\big(Y_n^{\circ R}\big)\big)\ge\Omega\big(Rlog\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big). \end{array}\right.\)

Combining these inequalities, we obtain

\(\alpha\big(n,\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(Y_n^{\circ R})\big)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{R}\big)\big)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\overline{\mathsf{Alt}}(Y_n^{\circ R})}\big)\big)\ge\Omega\big(log\big(\frac{logn}{\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(Y_n^{\circ R})}\big)\big).\)

It is easy to verify that \(\overline{\mathsf{OPT}}(Y_n^{\circ R})\) can range from _O_(1) to \(\Omega(logn)\) and that the available values spaced by at most a constant factor. \(\blacktriangleleft\)

## 5 Superadditivity of the Funnel Bound

We prove Theorem 20 in this section.

**Proof of Theorem 20.** The proof is mostly by picture (see Figure 6). Take some point _p_=(_x,t_) in _G<sub>X</sub>_, the geometric view of _X_. Its funnel will include:

Its _external funnel_: the points corresponding to its funnel from \(\widetilde{X}\).<sup>10</sup> This is because e.g. if \(j\in[l]\) is the most recent access that’s close to _j<sub>x</sub>_ on its left side, then the corresponding access in the composed sequence will definitely be the most recent access that’s close to _x_ on its left side, too.

Its _internal funnel_: the accesses corresponding to its funnel points from _X_<sup>(_j<sub>x</sub>_)</sup>.<sup>11</sup> This is because e.g. if \(y\in S_{j_x}\) is the most recent access that’s close to _x_ on its left side, then the other sequences _X_<sup>(_j_)</sup> for \(j\neq j_x\) are not going to interfere with that.

And maybe some extra funnel points.

In addition, all points of the external funnel are later in time than all points of the internal funnel. Suppose by contradiction there is an internal funnel point (_x<sub>I</sub>,t<sub>I</sub>_) that comes later than an external funnel point (_x<sub>E</sub>,t<sub>E</sub>_), i.e., _t<sub>I</sub>\>t<sub>E</sub>_. Also assume w.l.o.g. that _j<sub>x<sub>E</sub></sub>\<j<sub>x</sub>_. This means in \(G_\widetilde{X}\) we must have _j<sub>x</sub>=j<sub>xi<sub>I</sub></sub>_, then it means the point (_j<sub>xi<sub>I</sub></sub>,t<sub>I</sub>_) is in the rectangle formed by (_j<sub>x</sub>,t_) and (_j<sub>x<sub>E</sub></sub>,t<sub>E</sub>_) since _t\>t<sub>I</sub>\>t<sub>E</sub>_ and _j<sub>x</sub>=j<sub>xi<sub>I</sub></sub>\>j<sub>x<sub>E</sub></sub>_, and this contradicts with the definition that (_j<sub>x<sub>E</sub></sub>,t<sub>E</sub>_) is a funnel point in \(G_\widetilde{X}\).

<sup>10</sup> Or, more precisely, corresponding to the funnel of (_j<sub>x</sub>,t_) in the geometric view \(G_\widetilde{X}\). <sup>11</sup> Or, more precisely, corresponding to the funnel of \((x,\sigma(t))\) in the geometric view _G_<sub>_X_(_j<sub>x</sub>_)</sub>, where \(\sigma\) is defined as in Definition 17.

So every side switch between consecutive points of the external funnel gives at least one side switch in the combined funnel, and so does every side switch between consecutive points of the internal funnel, and there is no double counting.

## A Proof of Lemma 4

In this section, we prove Lemma 4. The intuition is we essentially use Tango-trees but the reference tree is split into levels according to the parameter. Our algorithm is based on bootstrapping the Tango tree of [16]. We remark that the main difference is that our algorithm is defined by a parameter \(k\in[1,\mathrm{log}n]\) (where we use the balanced BST to

implement the split/join operations in the preferred paths of Tango trees) whereas the (properly implemented) Tango tree of [16] is oblivious to the parameter.

Consider any fixed access sequence \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_m)\in S^m\). W.l.o.g. assume _n_=|_S_| is a power of 2, and we associate each key in _S_ with an integer in [_n_]. In this section, we will consider a fixed parameter _k_ that is an integer in [1,log_n_].

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 28** (perfect binary tree and subtrees)**.** _Let_ T _denote the perfect binary tree on_ [_n]._<sup>13</sup> _For each key_ \(x\in[n]\)_, define h<sub>x</sub> to be the depth of the node x in_ T _(root has depth_ 1_). Divide the tree_ T _into_ log_n/k levels such that the subtrees on each level have height k. For each key_ \(x\in[n]\)_, consider the path from the root to the node x, and we denote the subtrees encountered along this path as_ \(\mathcal{T}_1^{(x)},\cdots,\mathcal{T}_{\lceil h_x/k\rceil}^{(x)}\).

Note that each tree \(\mathcal{T}_\ell^{(x)}\) has height _k_.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 29** (preferred child and preferred path [15])**.** _At any time i, for any node x in_ T _, we define its preferred child to be the left (or right) child if the last access to a node within x’s subtree was in the left (or right) subtree of x. Each subtree of_ T _can be decomposed into disjoint sets of preferred paths by recursively following the preferred child._

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Definition 30** (number of changed preferred children)**.** _At any time i, and for any_ \(\ell\in[\lceil h_{X_i}/k\rceil]\)_, define_ \(a_\ell^{(X_i)}\) _to be the number of nodes in_ \(\mathcal{T}_\ell^{(X_i)}\) _whose preferred child changes during access of X<sub>i</sub>. Define_ \(a^{(X_i)}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\lceil h_{X_i}/k\rceil} a_\ell^{(X_i)}\) _to be the number of all nodes in the whole tree whose preferred child changes during access of X<sub>i</sub>._

By the definition of the alternation bound in Definition 13, we directly have the following lemma.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 31** (alternation bound)**.** Alt\(_\mathcal{T}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^ma^{(X_i)}\).

Similar to the original tango tree in [15], we maintain each preferred path as an auxiliary tree. Since we define a preferred path to be a path _within a subtree_, in the auxiliary tree we store the depth of a node _with respect to that subtree_ instead of its depth with respect to the whole tree T . We use the following result from [15]:

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 32** (auxiliary tree, Section 3.2 of [15])**.** _The auxiliary tree data structure is an augmented BST that stores a preferred path and supports "search", "cut by depth", and "join" operations. Each operation takes O_(log_p_+1) _time, where p is the total number of nodes in the preferred path._

**Algorithm.**

Now we are ready to describe our algorithm. Our data structure is an augmented BST that consists of all the auxiliary trees of all the preferred paths.

When accessing _X<sub>i</sub>_, the algorithm follows the BST until it reaches _X<sub>i</sub>_. Whenever a preferred child is changed, we use the "cut by depth", and "join" operations to change the auxiliary trees accordingly.

<sup>13</sup> Since each node of T uniquely stores a key in [_n_], with an abuse of notation, we will use _x_ to denote both a key in [_n_] and a node in the tree T.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 33** (time of one access)**.** _The time to search for X<sub>i</sub> is_

\(O\big((a^{(X_i)}+\frac{logn}{k})\cdot(logk+1)\big).\)

**Proof.** We first compute the time that the algorithm spends within a subtree \(\mathcal{T}_\ell^{(X_i)}\) for any \(\ell\in[\lceil h_{X_i}/k\rceil]\). Since \(\mathcal{T}_\ell^{(X_i)}\) has height _k_, the cost of each operation of an auxiliary tree is _O_(log_k_+1). The algorithm needs to make at least one search operation in one auxiliary tree, and apart from this, the algorithm also needs to make _O_(1) operations whenever a preferred child is changed, so the search time of _X<sub>i</sub>_ within the subtree \(\mathcal{T}_\ell^{(X_i)}\) is

\(O\big((a_\ell^{(X_i)}+1)(1+logk)\big).\)

Thus the total search time of _X<sub>i</sub>_ is

\(\sum_{\ell=1}^{\lceil h_{X_i}/k\rceil} O\big((a_\ell^{(X_i)}+1)(1+logk)\big)=O\big((a^{(X_i)}+\frac{logn}{k})\cdot(logk+1)\big),\)

where we used the fact that \(h_{X_i}\le logn\) and \(a^{(X_i)}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\lceil h_{X_i}/k\rceil} a_\ell^{(X_i)}\). \(\blacktriangleleft\)

Since \(\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^ma^{(X_i)}\), we can easily compute the total access time.

\(\blacktriangleright\) **Lemma 34** (total time)**.** _The total access time of the sequence_ \(X=(X_1,\cdots,X_m)\) _is_

\(O\big((\mathsf{Alt}_\mathcal{T}(X)+m\cdot\frac{logn}{k})\cdot(logk+1)\big).\)
